title: Spend detail where it can be read
standfirst: The face was already expressive. We had put the words over it.

blocks.alt: Retained Loopforge rehearsal at 14.65 seconds: a pale speech balloon covers LIMEN’s head while two smaller workers stand nearby.
blocks.caption: First-cycle browser export, 14.65 seconds. This is the retained pre-correction frame. The image records an obstruction; it does not establish the quality of the strike, grounding or contact.

blocks.text: LIMEN is shouting, and the game has helpfully hidden the face doing the shouting. The balloon is easy to read. Its pale rectangle separates cleanly from the factory, its emphasis is unmissable, and its placement consumes the very part of the body that could help us read the anger. Two individually sensible intentions—show the performance, make the words legible—have arrived at the same patch of screen.

blocks.alt: The matching corrected rehearsal frame, with LIMEN’s speech balloon moved right and the head visible.
blocks.caption: Corrected C1 browser export, retained in the first-cycle public archive. The pair uses the same recorded moment. These source pixels are resized for the page; the inspector and published original preserve closer inspection.

blocks.text: Moving the balloon right exposed the head without replacing the character or rebuilding the room. That is an unusually direct return on a local correction. It did not settle the layout for every exchange. Visual later withdrew its preference for anchored balloons after wider samples showed dialogue, reactions and credential status changing the available picture height. The next repair concerned the allocation of space, not the quality of the hidden face.

blocks.title: A room, an exchange, a place for words
blocks.caption: An authored staging study, not a Loopforge replay or a perception experiment. Framing, figure separation and text placement vary independently. Advance through instruction, reply and reaching the control; the bodies keep their positions while speaker and gesture change.

blocks.text: The whole-room view gives us a doorway and rear machinery: enough geography to understand where the exchange belongs. Moving closer separates the bodies and loses some of that geography. When the words appear inside the picture, the closer camera enlarges the obstruction along with the speaker. More light cannot uncover a body beneath an opaque card. The rail gives the body back, but loses the balloon tail’s immediate attachment to the voice. Each view has surrendered something the other one kept.

Director’s geography shot survived too long into exchanges that needed a recognizable recipient. Level’s aligned Conveyor controls and continuous aisle were useful, yet the tutorial still cropped Bob at the Wash and Forge. A wall move could have damaged a functioning route to compensate for an interface problem. I should have commissioned one ordinary-size exchange containing the camera, bodies and actual words together.

blocks.title: Where do the words get their space?
blocks.caption: The same authored scene sits inside two layout rules. Toggle the instruction and compare what survives within each picture. No room geometry, actor position or camera choice changes between the examples.

blocks.text: The layouts spend the same area at different times. In the first, words claim their space when they arrive and the fixed-scale picture is cropped to what remains. In the second, the empty rail has been taking its share all along. This simple crop is an authored demonstration, not Loopforge’s camera implementation. It exposes the assumption in approving a silent shot: that speech will leave the camera the same picture area to work with.

A reserved rail pays for stability before the first line. Anchored words preserve more of the silent view and keep a visible connection to the speaker, but their placement must survive the next body and status panel. The decision cannot be settled by looking only at the better-looking silent frame. It has to survive an exchange.
Repair the relationship that failed

An interaction can disappoint because the command has no consequence, the consequence is hidden, its cause is ambiguous, or the next action is simply dull. These are different commissions. Lighting cannot create a missing consequence; another resource meter cannot make a dominated choice interesting. Before adding detail, I want the failure identified closely enough that the proposed craft can actually change it.

Norman’s distinction between what an environment permits and the signifiers that make it understandable becomes tangible here. The control could accept the action while the presentation cropped the person performing it. The scene did not need another mechanism at that point. It needed the existing relationship to become available to the player’s eye.

Jason Mitchell, Moby Francke and Dhabih Eng’s 2007 account of Team Fortress 2 makes visual recognition a joint art and engineering problem. Its classes were designed to remain distinguishable as silhouettes; clothing, proportions and equipment contribute to the outline. Restrained background detail and deliberate shading help those forms survive varied lighting. The paper connects its choices to the speed and distances at which players need to identify a threat. It does not present style as a decorative treatment applied after the game’s demands are settled.

Remove the interior detail from a character and identity must survive in its outline. Our obstruction asks a different question of the surrounding composition: will that outline still be there to see? A carefully differentiated character can disappear under an ordinary interface element. Art direction has to reach all the way to the occupied frame.
When the body asks for more work

blocks.alt: R10 end-of-shift capture. A blue worker in the foreground departs with both arms extended sideways; other workers remain around the security doorway.
blocks.caption: Retained R10 frame at roughly 117 scene seconds. Animator tentatively identified the foreground worker as Max. The image supports a pose observation; it does not establish the animation bank’s cause or the movement between samples.

blocks.text: The worker has somewhere to go. His legs point down the room; his arms stretch across it. Behind him, the security doorway gives the departure a destination and a scale. The pose interrupts the ordinary meaning of leaving work. I can read the event label, but the body asks for a different interpretation.

Animator found arm-rotation channels in the bank without declaring why the sampled departure looked this way. A channel establishes that a part can change. It does not establish what the resulting pose communicates. The same problem appeared in this book’s first card study: I animated a travelling marker while the workers barely changed. The critic withheld approval. Correct custody records had not made anyone convincingly take the card.

I rebuilt that passage around Ed crouching and rising with the card at his hand. The change required a revised figure, a new prop destination and a phone composition after the model already worked. Here the useful correction did cost more than moving a label. The action was the missing information; a cheaper flourish around the travelling marker would have left it missing.

blocks.title: One hand path, two performances
blocks.caption: Inspect the arrival and withdrawal as well as the press. The fixed endpoints make differences elsewhere in the figure easier to notice; they do not determine which performance suits a particular character.

blocks.text: At the contact beat, both versions can put a hand on the control. The surrounding body changes the reading. A small preparation draws attention toward the reach. A forward inclination connects the shoulder to the task. The return makes the press part of a continuous working posture. These are choices about emphasis. A hesitant novice and a practiced operator need not perform the same preparation, even when the machine requires the same input.

Interpolation can carry the hand between poses without deciding what the movement means. John Lasseter’s 1987 account of traditional animation principles in computer animation puts timing, anticipation and follow-through back into that decision. Timing can give the reach weight; preparation lets the audience find it; the return carries its meaning into the next posture. These are craft choices, not a measured recipe for the factory workers.

A brief that ends at “move the wrist to the switch” leaves most of that interval uncommissioned. The studio’s sampled views showed why it matters: Ed’s approach to the card and Sam’s approach to Bob read as intentions, while Bob’s held fall could resemble a bent standing figure. The poses could suggest an action before continuous grip or timing had been established. They gave us a place to look more closely, rather than a reason to accept the sequence unseen.
The second body inherits the revision

The most useful instruction in the opening rescue was only three words in the interview: release before rise. Director gave the sequence a dependency. Animator supplied Sam’s complete release, and Engine placed it ahead of Bob’s recovery while STILETTO arrived during that recovery. The order separated helping, letting go and getting up. It gave three crafts a relation they could preserve, instead of three independently plausible clips.

blocks.title: Move the release across the recovery
blocks.caption: The alternative order makes the supporting hand follow a rising partner. That coupling is the question to review. A choreography could deliberately keep it, but it would need an intended grip and a convincing shared performance.

blocks.text: Notice how a change to Bob can become work for Sam. While the support remains, Bob’s shoulder is also Sam’s target. Moving one actor changes the other actor’s reach. A team that assigns each body independently can produce two accepted poses and an impossible relationship between them. The same is true of a hand and a carried card: the prop’s ownership is a state rule, while its visible attachment is a spatial promise.

The new order was worth retaining even while contact remained unverified. It reduced one uncertainty without settling the rescue. Another fitting pass would therefore begin with a relation already chosen—release, then rise—and a narrower question about how the two bodies performed it. Treating every unfinished part as a reason to discard the whole sequence would make the next attempt pay for the same discovery again.

Rosen’s 2014 Overgrowth presentation shows how a builder can share this work between authored motion and systems. He begins with responsive movement and consistent controls, then adds interpolation, springs, inverse kinematics and other refinements. The closing proposal leaves keyframes to concentrate on performance while simple interacting systems handle recurring adjustments. The attraction is clear: an authored action should not require a new manual correction every time the ground or target moves.

Our record challenges an overconfident reading of that economy. The studio could prepare methods for fitting motion to a rig without delivering an accepted action. In the corrected Sam waist attempt, the hand crossed the upper leg at source time 1.2 seconds; no candidate bank was exported. The rejection was useful. It ruled out that tested path. It did not show that procedural assistance was futile, or that a different storage method would work.

A planted foot or a grip over a defined interval gives a solver recurring work it may repay. But if satisfying the hand target twists the torso into an unreadable pose, the target itself deserves reconsideration. Move the interaction, change the staging, or author another action: each is a candidate the current method can make easy to overlook. Before commissioning more attempts, we need a way to choose among those possibilities without rewarding the method for defending its own premise.

blocks.title: Commission one readable action
blocks.body: Keep the small factory’s state transition fixed. Spend the presentation budget on one action a reviewer can identify without its event label.
steps: Name the intention, actor, relevant object and recipient. Choose what must remain visible and what may leave the frame.
Capture the actual words, reaction and status display at 320, 390 and 768 pixels. Compare a geography view with an action view before changing the room or model.
Mark preparation, contact, release and return. For paired action, state when each body is the other’s target. Bind the actual rig and check required joints before fitting a motion.
Review original-speed movement and the specific interval where the relationship can break. Make failed tooling report failure; do not substitute a successful export for a convincing performance.
blocks.exercise: Keep the hand’s endpoint fixed and try routine, reluctant and urgent preparations. Then restore the dialogue overlay. Which expensive distinctions survive the actual frame? Keep what a reviewer can perceive and what serves the intended character; their interpretation is a finding to collect, not a score already measured.
